metadata.title: PISA 2015 Results (Volume V): Collaborative Problem Solving

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This volume reports PISA 2015 results based on a complex, multi-stage sampling design of 15-year-old students within participating countries and economies. The report explains that sampling and weighting operations were led by Westat and that sampling errors are used to quantify uncertainty in country mean estimates. For school-level questionnaire responses, the report states that principal responses are weighted to be proportionate to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in the school. The excerpt provided does not specify the exact student weight variable name(s) (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or whether replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) were used; therefore, the weighting implementation details are not fully recoverable from the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is an OECD/PISA results volume that reports proficiency distributions and relationships using PISA scaling and index construction procedures, but the provided excerpt does not document a specific, analysis-level plausible-values strategy (e.g., Rubin combining rules) for the collaborative problem-solving scale. Missing-data handling is also not described at the level of an explicit analytic procedure (e.g., listwise deletion vs multiple imputation) in the excerpt. As a result, the missing-data handling cannot be classified from the supplied text without the technical annex sections that detail index construction and missing observations.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report targets 15-year-old students (15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months) enrolled in grade 7 or above, with exclusions applied using internationally established PISA criteria (e.g., intellectual disability or limited proficiency in the language of assessment). For this volume, collaborative problem solving was administered only in the subset of countries/economies that participated in the computer-based collaborative problem-solving assessment; the excerpt notes that the collaborative problem-solving assessment was not conducted in several systems that delivered PISA 2015 on paper and was also not conducted in specific countries/economies (e.g., Dominican Republic, Ireland, Poland, Qatar, Switzerland). The excerpt does not provide the exact student-level analytic inclusion/exclusion rules for the collaborative problem-solving scale beyond the general PISA exclusion framework.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA 2015 Results (Volume V) volume reports international comparisons for the first large-scale assessment of collaborative problem solving. The assessment is computer-based and administered to 15-year-olds across participating countries and economies, with test items organized into clusters and delivered in consecutive clusters per domain; students complete a two-hour assessment including science, reading, mathematics, and collaborative problem solving where applicable. The report describes PISA’s scaling approach and 2015 methodological changes (e.g., hybrid Rasch/2-parameter scaling, consistent treatment of non-reached items, and multiple-cycle scaling) to generate proficiency estimates reported as proficiency levels and distributions. Results are presented as country/economy means, proficiency-level shares (e.g., low achievers and top performers), and relationships with student demographics, attitudes, and school/classroom factors. The excerpt does not specify an analysis-level missing-data or plausible-values procedure for the collaborative problem-solving outcomes, so technical details must be taken from the technical annexes referenced in the volume.
